title: Do as the locals do
goals: Describe how traditional things are made, sold and celebrated, using the passive voice (is made of, are held, was built).
Talk about manners and customs: what is polite, rude or acceptable in different countries.
Use verb + -ing as a subject and after prepositions (Eating in public is rude; by learning the customs).
Give behavior advice with It's + adjective + (not) to + verb, understanding how the meaning changes depending on where not goes.
Give your opinion frankly and firmly (To be honest, …; I'd absolutely miss…) and avoid an abrupt of course.
Write about traditions and give advice to a foreign visitor.

learn.title: Passive voice in the simple present
learn.html:
We use the passive when we don't know who does the action, or when it doesn't matter. In Spanish we often use a 'se' construction for this. In English it is simply They are made by hand. In English we almost always need the subject and be + past participle.

Active: They carve the sculptures out of ice. → Passive: The sculptures are carved out of ice. If the agent does matter, add by: The sculptures are carved by teams from all over the world.

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativesubject + is / are + participleKim-bap is made with rice and vegetables.
Negativesubject + is / are + not + participleIt's not eaten hot.
Question with a question wordWh- + is / are + subject + participleHow is kim-bap made?
Yes/no questionIs / Are + subject + participleIs it eaten hot or cold?
  • Singular subject → is; plural → are: The festival is held…, Crafts are sold…
  • Only verbs with a direct object have a passive form; happen, arrive or take place do not form it.

watch.why: Be + past participle, not the base form.

watch.right: The festival is held in November.
watch.why: The festival doesn't 'celebrate': it is celebrated. It needs is + held.

watch.wrong: Is made this cheese in Oaxaca?
watch.right: Is this cheese made in Oaxaca?
watch.why: In the question, is goes before the subject and the participle goes after it.
-ing is the present continuous; the passive uses the past participle.

learn.title: Passive in the past and with modals
learn.html:
The same idea extends to other tenses: we change be and keep the past participle. This is the bridge to a more formal, written English (guides, news, instructions).

FormStructureExample
Simple pastwas / were + past participleThe cathedral was built in 1750. The masks were painted by local artists.
Futurewill be + past participleThe results will be announced on Friday.
With modalscan / must / should + be + past participleShoes must be taken off at the door. This soup can be served cold.
  • With modals, be takes the base form: must be taken, NOT must taken.
  • by + agent only if it matters: The mural was painted by Diego Rivera.

watch.right: Shoes must be taken off here.
watch.why: With modals: modal + be + past participle.

watch.wrong: The festival was happened in May.
watch.right: The festival took place in May. / The festival was held in May.
watch.why: Happen has no passive; use took place or was held.

watch.wrong: The mural was painted from Rivera.
watch.right: The mural was painted by Rivera.
watch.why: The agent is introduced with by.

learn.title: Verb + -ing as a subject and after prepositions
learn.html:
In Spanish we often use the infinitive as the subject, for example 'comer en público es de mala educación'. In English, the subject is a verb with -ing (gerund), and the main verb goes in the singular.

UseStructureExample
Subjectverb-ing + isEating in public is bad manners.
Negative subjectnot + verb-ing + isNot shaking hands is impolite.
After a prepositionby / for / without / instead of + verb-ingYou can offend people by eating in public.
Preposition + negativeby / for + not + verb-ingPeople might stare at you for not shaking hands.
  • by + -ing = the means or manner: You make friends by learning the customs.
  • for + -ing = the reason: He was criticized for arriving late.
  • After ANY preposition you use -ing, never the infinitive: without leaving a tip, instead of waiting.

watch.why: Subject: verb with -ing, and the main verb in the singular.

watch.wrong: You can offend people for eat with your hands.
watch.right: You can offend people by eating with your hands.

watch.why: Not + verb with -ing as the subject.

watch.wrong: They stared at me for no shaking hands.
watch.right: They stared at me for not shaking hands.
watch.why: Negating a gerund: not + -ing, not no.

learn.title: It's + adjective + to + verb, and the position of not
learn.html:
To talk about behavior, we use It's + adjective / noun + to + verb: It's bad manners to eat in public. The subject It is required (in Spanish the subject is often left out). To negate the action: not + to + verb: It's impolite not to shake hands.

Not goes right before what it negates. Changing its position changes the meaning:

SentenceMeaning
It's acceptable not to tip cab drivers.It's optional: you don't have to leave a tip.
It's not acceptable to tip cab drivers.You shouldn't do it: it's frowned upon.
Be careful not to point at people.Avoid pointing at people.
You can offend people by not bowing.You offend people if you don't bow.

Useful adjectives: rude, impolite, polite, acceptable, inappropriate, customary, normal, bad manners.

watch.wrong: It's impolite eat with your mouth full.
watch.right: It's impolite to eat with your mouth full.
watch.why: After It's + adjective comes to + verb.

watch.wrong: Is rude to point at people.
watch.right: It's rude to point at people.
watch.why: The subject It is required in English.
The negation is not, not no.

watch.wrong: It's bad manners for eat with your hands.
watch.right: It's bad manners to eat with your hands.
watch.why: After an adjective or noun that expresses an opinion, use to + verb, not for + -ing.

learn.title: Strategy: sounding more direct
learn.html:
To give your opinion firmly, or to be more frank, add an adverb or phrase at the beginning of the sentence:

  • absolutely, certainly, definitely, really, actually, honestly — go before the main verb: I'd absolutely miss the food.
  • in fact, to be honest, to tell you the truth — open the sentence: To be honest, I don't miss too much.

Be careful with “of course”: it means “it's what you'd expect” and is used to show agreement (A: I really miss my family. B: Of course.). But as a reply to a question it can sound abrupt or rude: A: Do you miss your family? B: Oh, yes, I really do. (NOT Of course.)

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• One of my favorite proverbs is … — introduce a proverb.
  • It's often said when … — explain when it is used.
  • It means that … — give its meaning.
  • A similar proverb in English is … — compare it with another language.
  • I like it because … — give your reason.
  • It's customary to … / It's bad manners to … — talk about customs.
  • To be honest, … / To tell you the truth, … / In fact, … — give your opinion frankly.

write.prompt: Write a 180 to 250-word text about the traditions and customs of your city or country for a foreign visitor. Include: (1) at least three things that are made, sold or celebrated, using the passive voice (is made of, are sold, is held…); (2) two sentences with verb + -ing as a subject; (3) two sentences with It's + adjective + (not) to + verb; (4) one expression to sound more direct (To be honest, …). Example opening: Mexico is famous for its traditions. For example, …
checklist: Between 180 and 250 words
At least 3 passive sentences (is / are / was / were + past participle)
Correct past participles (made, sold, held, built)
Two subjects with -ing and the main verb in the singular
Two sentences with It's + adjective + to + verb (one with not to)
by + -ing to say how
At least one expression such as To be honest or In fact
write.model:
Mexico is famous for its traditions. For example, tequila is made from the blue agave plant in the state of Jalisco, and mole is served at weddings and festivals. Colorful crafts are sold in markets across the country, and every November the Day of the Dead is celebrated with flowers, candles and food. In my city, a big festival was held last year, and a new square was built for the occasion.

If you visit, remember that eating late is normal here. Having lunch around three o'clock is common, and sharing food with other people is a sign of friendship. Trying new dishes is a good way to be polite. It's important to say hello when you enter a shop, and it's not polite to refuse food at someone's home. It's nice to bring a small gift, but it's not necessary to spend a lot. It's better not to arrive too early at a party.

You can learn a lot about the culture by walking around the old center, or by talking with the vendors. By asking questions, you will make friends quickly. To be honest, we are not always on time, so it's good to be patient. In fact, being late is almost normal for parties. Don't take it personally!

I hope you enjoy your visit, and that you leave with beautiful memories.

Write an email of 180 to 250 words with manners advice: greetings, tipping, meals and visiting homes. Use vocabulary from the unit (shake hands, leave a tip, take your shoes off, keep your voice down) and explain what is acceptable, what is bad manners and why. Example opening: Hi Jake, I'm happy you're coming to Mexico! Here is some advice …
targets: It's acceptable not to / It's not acceptable to
checklist: Between 180 and 250 words
Greeting and sign-off of the email
At least 4 manners verbs or phrases from the unit
At least one sentence with -ing as the subject
A correct contrast between acceptable not to and not acceptable to
One sentence with by or for + (not) + -ing
One passive sentence (e.g., tips are expected / shoes are taken off)
write.model:
Hi Jake,

I'm happy you're coming to Mexico! Here is some advice so you can feel comfortable.

When you meet someone, shake hands and look the person in the eye. Close friends usually greet each other with a kiss on the cheek, so don't be surprised. Saying hello to everyone in a room is expected, and ignoring people is bad manners.

In restaurants, it's customary to leave a tip of around ten percent, and tips are often expected even in small places. Of course, it's acceptable not to tip if the service was terrible, but it's not acceptable to complain loudly. Keep your voice down in public places, because speaking loudly is considered rude.

If someone invites you to their home, bring a small present, like flowers or sweets. Take your shoes off only if the host asks you to. Shoes are not always taken off, so watch what others do. Meals are long, and it's polite to wait until the host says "provecho" before you start eating. By saying thank you for the food, you will make a great impression. Nobody will be offended if you do not finish everything, but it's better to try a bit of each dish.

I think you will love it here. Write to me if you have any questions!

Best,
Luis

reading.title: Two sets of customs
reading.intro: Read the text by a Mexican student who lived in Korea for a year, then answer the questions.
paragraphs: When I moved to Busan for a graduate program, I thought I was well prepared. I had read three guidebooks, learned a hundred words of Korean, and even packed a jar of mole paste. What I had not studied was manners, and that was a mistake. Nobody warned me that some of the smallest habits would turn out to be the most important ones. I was sure that a friendly attitude and a few polite phrases would be enough, but I soon discovered that good intentions are not the same as good manners.

On my first day, my host mother greeted me at the door. I held out my hand, but she bowed slightly, and I felt embarrassed. Shaking hands is normal in Mexico, yet in many Korean homes a small bow is more customary. Then came the shoes. Shoes are always taken off at the entrance, and slippers are provided for guests. Walking around the house in my boots would have been a disaster, and my host mother kindly pretended not to notice my confusion.

Restaurants taught me even more. In Mexico, leaving a tip of ten or fifteen percent is expected; in Korea it usually is not, and it can even confuse the waiter. Meals are often shared, and the oldest person is served first. It's impolite to start eating before the eldest person at the table picks up a spoon. I also learned that pouring a drink for yourself is not done: you fill other people's glasses, and they fill yours. Not following this custom will not make you a criminal, but people may smile at you for ignoring it.

Of course, my country has customs that surprise visitors, too. My Korean friends were shocked that tortillas are eaten with the hands, that a long family lunch is held on Sundays, and that it is normal to greet friends with a kiss on the cheek. One friend told me, "To be honest, I was nervous the first time. I didn't know where to put my face!" Honestly, I laughed so hard that I forgot my own embarrassment.

After a year abroad, I have changed my mind about manners. They are not silly rules; they are a language without words. Learning a few of them shows respect, and showing respect is the fastest way to make friends. I still feel homesick sometimes, especially when I smell fresh bread, but now I carry two sets of customs with me. If you move abroad, my advice is simple: watch, ask, and don't be afraid to make a mistake.

lines.text: Kenji, I'm having dinner at my manager's house on Friday. Is there anything I should know?
Congratulations! First, shoes are always taken off at the door, so wear nice socks.
Good tip. Should I bring a gift?
Yes. It's customary to bring something small, like fruit or sweets. And the gift is usually given with both hands.
Both hands? Interesting. What about the meal?
Don't start eating before the host does. Starting early is impolite.
Got it. And what about tipping the taxi driver afterwards?
Honestly, tipping isn't expected in Japan. It's acceptable not to tip, and some drivers even feel uncomfortable about it.
That's the opposite of Mexico! Anything else?
Yes, one more thing. Sticking chopsticks upright in your rice is a serious mistake. It's connected with funerals.
Wow, I definitely didn't know that. Thanks for the help.

tasks.model: A traditional dish from my region is mole. It is made with chocolate, chilies and spices, and it is served with chicken and rice. It's cooked for weddings and big family parties. In my town, a festival is held every October, and handmade crafts are sold in the main square. They are made of clay and wood.
checklist: is / are + past participle
made of / made with / made out of
held for events
A clear subject in each sentence

tasks.prompt: Talk about good and bad manners in Mexico. Use -ing as a subject and It's + adjective + to.
questions: What is bad manners in your country?
Is it acceptable not to leave a tip?
What can you do to be polite when you meet someone?
What is a custom that surprises visitors?
tasks.model: In Mexico, cutting in line is rude. Leaving a tip is customary, and it's not acceptable to forget it. It's polite to say hello when you enter a shop. Talking loudly on the metro is bad manners, so keep your voice down. Visitors are often surprised that we greet friends with a kiss on the cheek.
checklist: -ing as a subject with a singular verb
It's + adjective + to + verb
Correct use of not
Manners vocabulary

tasks.prompt: Talk about living or traveling abroad and what you would miss from home. Sound direct with expressions from the unit.
questions: Would you like to live abroad? Why or why not?
What would you miss from home?
What would you do to make friends in a new country?
tasks.model: To be honest, I'd love to live abroad for a year. I'd definitely miss my family and the food, of course. I'd feel homesick in the winter. To tell you the truth, I think I would make friends by joining a class and learning the local customs.
checklist: To be honest / To tell you the truth
definitely / absolutely before the verb
by + -ing
feel homesick / miss
